messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Before the assault, Amara had been known for her steady hand and her willingness to step into the middle of any dispute. She was a patrol officer in a mid-sized city, and she had always prided herself on her ability to de-escalate. That changed on a cool October night when she responded to a domestic disturbance call. The suspect, a man she had encountered before, ambushed her in the stairwell of the building. He overpowered her, pinned her against the concrete wall, and sexually assaulted her while she was still wearing her duty belt. She remembers the pressure of his forearm against her throat, the cold bite of the wall against her back, and the sound of her own radio crackling uselessly on the floor. But there are parts she cannot retrieve—the exact sequence of how he got her weapon away from her, the moment she lost consciousness, the faces of the neighbors who eventually found her. Those gaps haunt her more than the pieces she can recall.

When the memory returns now, it arrives with a searing physical pain in her lower back and shoulders, exactly where she was pressed into the wall. The pain is so vivid that she has been to three different doctors, none of whom found any injury. Alongside the pain comes a wave of rage so intense that her hands shake. She has come to believe that she has permanently changed for the worse, that the person she was before the assault is gone. This conviction shapes her daily life. Amara is certain that somebody else—a better officer, a stronger woman—would not have gotten into that situation in the first place. She has also lost her connection to her community and culture; she no longer attends the Ghanaian church gatherings she once loved, because she is sure the other women there would see the shame in her eyes.

These appraisals have driven her to adopt rigid maladaptive strategies. She now avoids any situation that might involve disagreement or confrontation, a nearly impossible task for a police officer. She has requested desk duty, citing vague physical complaints, and her sergeant has noticed she no longer responds to calls that involve domestic disputes. At home, she avoids emotional stress entirely. She steers conversations with her husband toward neutral topics—schedules, groceries—and if he tries to ask how she is feeling, she finds a reason to leave the room. She also spends hours caught in counterfactual thinking, replaying the night and imagining how life would have been different if she had waited for backup, if she had called in sick that shift, if she had been a different kind of person entirely. This rumination is directly triggered by the memory gaps; the missing pieces feel like evidence that she failed to pay attention, that she was not the officer she thought she was. The rage on recall makes the counterfactuals even more punishing, because she imagines versions of the event where she fought back successfully, and the gap between that fantasy and her actual memory feels like proof of her own weakness.

A minor but persistent note: she sometimes notices her husband flinching when she walks into the kitchen unexpectedly, and she has begun to wonder if he is afraid of her now too. She does not connect this observation to anything else; it simply sits alongside her other burdens.

What finally brought Amara to seek help was a call she could not avoid. Last week, a dispatcher mistakenly routed her to a noise complaint at the same apartment complex. She drove there, parked three blocks away, and sat in her squad car for forty-five minutes, unable to get out. When she finally called for a unit swap, she had to lie and say she was feeling ill. Her partner did not question it, but she saw the look in his eyes. That evening, she told her husband she needed to see someone. She is most afraid that the therapist will confirm what she already believes: that she is permanently broken, that she can never go back on patrol, that she has become someone who cannot handle the very job that once defined her. But she is also, quietly, hoping that someone can help her remember what she has lost in those gaps—because she is certain that if she could just get those pieces back, she might finally stop feeling so lost.
